\chapter{More Good Manners}
\label{ch:te-more-manners}
\hlchaptermodality{65}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can welcome somebody in Telugu, make a request, ask their leave, and thank them.}

\section[svāgataṁ]{\te{స్వాగతం} (svāgataṁ) — a welcome}

\label{lesson:TE-C65-welcome}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{iṅkā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{స్వాగతం}}
\textbf{\te{స్వాగతం}} (\emph{svāgataṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a welcome\textquotedblright{}.

Keep this well apart from \te{పరవాలేదు}. \te{పరవాలేదు} is what you say after somebody thanks you. \te{స్వాగతం} is what you say when they walk in. English hands the one word \textquotedblleft{}welcome\textquotedblright{} both jobs; Telugu does not.

It is Sanskrit, and it comes apart neatly: \emph{su-} \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} and \emph{āgata} \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}well come\textquotedblright{}, which is what the English word is too, arrived by an entirely separate road.

A house says it with the door open and a \emph{gauravaṁ} behind it. The \te{ముగ్గు} at the step is the same sentence without any words in it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first thing said at a door.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{svāgataṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{svāgataṁ}, then \emph{paravālēdu}, and say which one answers a thank-you
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{స్వాగతం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a welcome\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maryāda]{\te{మర్యాద} (maryāda) — good manners}

\label{lesson:TE-C65-manners}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{svāgataṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మర్యాద}}
\textbf{\te{మర్యాద}} (\emph{maryāda}) — \textquotedblleft{}good manners\textquotedblright{}.

\te{మర్యాద} is the doing half of \emph{gauravaṁ}. Respect is what you feel for somebody; \te{మర్యాద} is what you do about it — standing up, offering the \te{కుర్చీ}, serving the \emph{atithi} before yourself.

The word is Sanskrit and its first sense was a boundary line. Manners as a line you do not step over is a picture worth keeping hold of.

\te{మర్యాదగా} is how it usually reaches a person: \te{మర్యాదగా} \te{మాట్లాడు}, \textquotedblleft{}speak with manners\textquotedblright{}, which sounds sterner in English than it does in Telugu. It is closer to \textquotedblleft{}be decent about it\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: what you feel and what you do.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maryāda}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maryāda}, then \emph{gauravaṁ}, and say which one somebody can watch you doing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మర్యాద} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}good manners\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[manavi]{\te{మనవి} (manavi) — a polite request}

\label{lesson:TE-C65-request}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maryāda} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మనవి}}
\textbf{\te{మనవి}} (\emph{manavi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a polite request\textquotedblright{}.

\te{మనవి} is a request made from below — not \te{దయచేసి} set in front of an instruction, but the whole thing framed as a submission. \te{ఒక} \te{మనవి}, \textquotedblleft{}one request\textquotedblright{}, is said before the request itself arrives.

Where the word came from is not something any source consulted here settles, so nothing is invented for it. What is certain is the register it sits in, and that is the part a learner needs.

A \te{మనవి} goes to somebody who can say no: an official, an elder, a host. The word does half the softening before you have said what you want.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{manavi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{manavi}, then \emph{dayacēsi}, and say which one is the whole request
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మనవి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a polite request\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anumati]{\te{అనుమతి} (anumati) — permission}

\label{lesson:TE-C65-permission}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{manavi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{అనుమతి}}
\textbf{\te{అనుమతి}} (\emph{anumati}) — \textquotedblleft{}permission\textquotedblright{}.

\te{అనుమతి} is permission — what a \te{మనవి} is hoping to be given. \te{అనుమతి} \te{ఇవ్వండి}, \textquotedblleft{}give permission\textquotedblright{}, is the formal shape of it; in a house it usually comes out as a nod.

It is Sanskrit: \emph{anu-} \textquotedblleft{}along with\textquotedblright{} and \emph{mati} \textquotedblleft{}a mind\textquotedblright{}. Permission is somebody's mind going along with yours, which is a kinder picture than the English word offers.

Asking leave before you go is where it is most used, and it sits naturally in front of \te{వెళ్ళొస్తాను}. With \te{అనుమతి} first, leaving stops being something you announce and becomes something you are given.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{anumati}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{anumati}, then \emph{veḷḷostānu}, and take your leave properly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{అనుమతి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}permission\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nammakaṁ]{\te{నమ్మకం} (nammakaṁ) — trust}

\label{lesson:TE-C65-trust}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{anumati} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నమ్మకం}}
\textbf{\te{నమ్మకం}} (\emph{nammakaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}trust\textquotedblright{}.

\te{నమ్మకం} is trust, and it is the one word here that is Telugu's own. It is built on \te{నమ్ము}, \textquotedblleft{}to believe\textquotedblright{}, with the ending that turns an action into the thing itself.

The four before it are Sanskrit and they are all about form: a welcome, manners, a request, permission. \te{నమ్మకం} is what the form is for. A house that does all four and is still not trusted has been doing something else.

The word also carries \textquotedblleft{}belief\textquotedblright{} in the religious sense, and Telugu is content to let one word hold both. Trusting a person and believing a thing are the same act pointed in two directions.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{స్వాగతం}, \te{మర్యాద}, \te{మనవి}, \te{అనుమతి}, \te{నమ్మకం}. Enough to bring somebody in, ask something of them, and say \te{ధన్యవాదములు} when they agree.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nammakaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say \emph{dhanyavādamulu} to whoever gave you the last one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నమ్మకం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}trust\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
